Groundnut___Leaf_Spot.description: Leaf Spot in Groundnut is caused by fungal pathogens including Cercospora arachidicola (Early Leaf Spot) and Cercosporidium personatum (Late Leaf Spot). It is the most common and destructive foliar disease of groundnut worldwide, causing significant yield loss if untreated.
Groundnut___Leaf_Spot.symptoms: Small, circular, dark brown to black spots on leaves. Early leaf spot produces spots on the upper leaf surface, while late leaf spot produces spots on both surfaces. Spots may have a yellow halo. Severe infections cause premature defoliation and reduced pod filling.
Groundnut___Leaf_Spot.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties. Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, tebuconazole, or mancozeb) at the first sign of disease. Practice crop rotation with non-host crops. Ensure proper plant spacing for air circulation. Remove and destroy crop debris after harvest.

Groundnut___Nutrition_Deficiency.description: Nutritional deficiencies in Groundnut commonly include iron chlorosis, zinc deficiency, and calcium deficiency. These can cause stunted growth, yellowing of leaves, and reduced yield.
Groundnut___Nutrition_Deficiency.symptoms: Iron deficiency: interveinal chlorosis on young leaves. Zinc deficiency: bronzing and stunting of leaflets. Calcium deficiency: poor root development and unfilled pods. Nitrogen deficiency: general yellowing of older leaves.
Groundnut___Nutrition_Deficiency.treatment_prevention: Conduct soil testing before planting. Apply balanced fertilizers based on soil test results. Use foliar sprays of micronutrients (iron sulfate, zinc sulfate) as needed. Ensure proper soil pH (5.5-7.0). Incorporate organic matter into the soil.

Groundnut___Rust.description: Groundnut Rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia arachidis. It can cause severe epidemics leading to defoliation and substantial yield losses. Both early rust and rust infections are grouped under this condition.
Groundnut___Rust.symptoms: Small, reddish-brown to orange pustules (uredinia) primarily on the undersides of leaves. Pustules may also appear on petioles and stems. Severe infections cause leaf yellowing, premature defoliation, stunted plant growth, and significant yield reduction.
Groundnut___Rust.treatment_prevention: Plant resistant varieties when available. Apply protectant fungicides (mancozeb, chlorothalonil) or systemic fungicides (triazoles) at the onset of symptoms. Practice crop rotation with non-host crops. Avoid dense planting to reduce humidity in the canopy. Remove volunteer groundnut plants that can harbor the fungus.

Pumpkin___bacterial_leaf_spot.description: Bacterial Leaf Spot in Pumpkin is caused by Xanthomonas cucurbitae. It affects pumpkin leaves, reducing photosynthesis and fruit quality. The bacteria can survive in plant debris and spread through water splash and contaminated tools.
Pumpkin___bacterial_leaf_spot.symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked lesions on leaves that turn brown to black. Lesions are often surrounded by a yellow halo. In severe cases, spots coalesce causing leaf blight and defoliation. Fruit may develop small, sunken, scab-like lesions.
Pumpkin___bacterial_leaf_spot.treatment_prevention: Use disease-free seeds and resistant varieties. Apply copper-based fungicides preventively. Practice crop rotation of 2-3 years with non-cucurbit crops. Avoid overhead irrigation. Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest.

Pumpkin___downy_mildew.description: Downy Mildew in Pumpkin is caused by the oomycete Pseudoperonospora cubensis. It is a destructive foliar disease that spreads rapidly in cool, humid conditions. The pathogen can cause significant yield losses if not managed promptly.
Pumpkin___downy_mildew.symptoms: Angular, yellow to pale green lesions on the upper leaf surface, bounded by leaf veins. Under high humidity, a gray to purple fuzzy growth appears on the underside of lesions. Infected leaves quickly turn brown and die, leading to defoliation.
Pumpkin___downy_mildew.treatment_prevention: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or metalaxyl) preventively in humid conditions. Use resistant varieties when available. Ensure proper plant spacing for air circulation. Avoid overhead irrigation. Remove crop debris after harvest.

Pumpkin___mosaic_disease.description: Mosaic Disease in Pumpkin is caused by several viruses including Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), and Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV). These viruses are transmitted by aphids and cause significant yield reduction.
Pumpkin___mosaic_disease.symptoms: Mottled light and dark green patterns (mosaic) on leaves. Leaves may be distorted, blistered, or reduced in size. Plants may be stunted. Fruits can be deformed with discolored, bumpy surfaces. Yellowing and leaf curling are common.
Pumpkin___mosaic_disease.treatment_prevention: Use virus-resistant varieties. Control aphid populations with insecticides or reflective mulches. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Practice crop rotation. Control weeds that can serve as virus reservoirs. Use certified disease-free seeds.

Pumpkin___powdery_mildew.description: Powdery Mildew in Pumpkin is caused by Podosphaera xanthii (formerly Sphaerotheca fuliginea). It is a common fungal disease that appears as white powdery growth on leaves, reducing photosynthesis and fruit quality.
Pumpkin___powdery_mildew.symptoms: White to gray powdery fungal growth on the upper surfaces of leaves, stems, and sometimes fruit. Affected leaves may yellow, turn brown, and die prematurely. Severe infection can lead to defoliation, sunburned fruit, and reduced yield.
Pumpkin___powdery_mildew.treatment_prevention: Apply sulfur-based or systemic fungicides (myclobutanil, trifloxystrobin) at the first sign of powdery growth. Plant resistant varieties. Ensure good air circulation through proper spacing. Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization. Remove and destroy infected plant debris.

Maize___Blight.description: Northern Leaf Blight on Maize is caused by Exserohilum turcicum. It produces large, cigar-shaped gray-green lesions on leaves that can significantly reduce photosynthesis and yield.
Maize___Blight.symptoms: Large, elliptical, grayish-green to tan lesions on leaves, typically 1-6 inches long. Lesions start on lower leaves and move upward. Severe infection causes leaf death and reduced grain fill.
Maize___Blight.treatment_prevention: Plant resistant hybrids, apply fungicides at early symptom onset, practice crop rotation with non-host crops, till crop residue to reduce inoculum, and avoid overhead irrigation.

Maize___Gray_Leaf_Spot.description: Gray leaf spot is caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis. It is one of the most damaging foliar diseases of maize in humid, warm regions.

Sugarcane___Rust.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties, apply foliar fungicides in severe cases, maintain balanced nutrition (especially potassium), and ensure adequate plant spacing for airflow.

Sugarcane___Yellow.treatment_prevention: Use virus-free planting material, plant resistant varieties, control aphid vectors, and use tissue-culture plantlets for clean seed stock.

Tomato___bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas species. It is highly contagious in warm, wet conditions.
Tomato___bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves. The centers of spots dry out and fall out, creating a 'shot-hole' appearance. Fruit develops raised, dark, scabby lesions.
Tomato___bacterial_spot.treatment_prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Apply copper-based bactericides early. Disinfect stakes and tools. Remove infected crop debris immediately.

Tomato___early_blight.description: Early blight is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. It targets solanaceous crops like tomatoes and potatoes.
Tomato___early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown, circular lesions with concentric rings ('target board') starting on older, lower leaves. Affected leaves yellow and drop off, exposing fruit to sunscald.
Tomato___early_blight.treatment_prevention: Mulch the soil to prevent soil-borne spores from splashing onto lower leaves. Prune lower leaves to improve airflow. Apply copper or chlorothalonil fungicides.

Tomato___healthy.treatment_prevention: Provide deep watering at the base of the plant. Apply balanced organic fertilizers. Prune suckers to improve airflow.

Tomato___late_blight.description: Late blight is a highly destructive disease caused by Phytophthora infestans, thriving in cool, wet weather.
Tomato___late_blight.symptoms: Large, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves and stems that expand rapidly and turn black. White fuzzy mold appears on leaf undersides in high humidity. Fruit develops large, firm, greasy brown blotches.
Tomato___late_blight.treatment_prevention: Grow resistant cultivars. Keep foliage dry (use drip irrigation). Space plants for air circulation. Immediately pull and bag infected plants to prevent spore release.

Wheat___Aphid.description: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that attack wheat crops. They cluster on leaves and stems, draining nutrients and weakening the plant. Heavy infestations can cause yellowing, stunted growth, and reduced grain yield.
Wheat___Aphid.symptoms: Yellowing and curling of leaves, sticky honeydew residue on leaf surfaces, presence of small green or black insects on the underside of leaves, stunted growth, and distorted leaf tips.
Wheat___Aphid.treatment_prevention: Use resistant wheat varieties, encourage natural predators like ladybugs and lacewings, apply insecticidal soap or neem oil for minor infestations, use systemic insecticides for severe outbreaks, and practice crop rotation.

Wheat___Black_Rust.description: Black rust, also known as stem rust, is caused by the fungus Puccinia graminis. It produces dark brown to black pustules on stems and leaf sheaths. It can cause significant yield losses by disrupting nutrient transport and weakening stems.
Wheat___Black_Rust.symptoms: Dark brown to black elongated pustules on stems, leaf sheaths, and occasionally leaves. Pustules rupture the epidermis and release dark reddish-brown spores. Severe infections cause premature leaf senescence, stem weakening, and lodging.
Wheat___Black_Rust.treatment_prevention: Plant resistant varieties, apply fungicides at early infection stages, destroy volunteer wheat and alternate hosts (barberry), practice crop rotation, and monitor fields regularly during warm, humid conditions.

Wheat___Blast.description: Wheat blast is caused by Magnaporthe oryzae pathotype Triticum. It is a devastating disease that causes bleaching of spikelets and can destroy entire heads. First identified in Brazil, now spreading globally.
Wheat___Blast.symptoms: Bleached, dry spikelets starting from the tip of the head. Lesions on leaves are initially small and diamond-shaped with gray centers and brown borders. Infected heads produce no grain.
Wheat___Blast.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties (primary control), apply fungicides preventively, avoid planting during warm and humid weather, practice crop rotation, and manage volunteer wheat plants.

Wheat___Brown_Rust.description: Brown rust is caused by Puccinia triticina and is the most common rust disease of wheat. It produces small, circular to oval orange-brown pustules primarily on the upper surface of leaves.
Wheat___Brown_Rust.symptoms: Small, circular to oval orange-brown pustules scattered across the upper leaf surface. Leaves may yellow and die prematurely. In severe cases, the disease reduces photosynthesis and grain filling.
Wheat___Brown_Rust.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties, apply foliar fungicides (triazoles or strobilurins) when disease appears, ensure adequate nutrition (especially nitrogen), avoid late planting, and practice crop rotation.

Wheat___Common_Root_Rot.description: Common root rot is caused by several soil-borne fungi including Bipolaris sorokiniana. It affects the roots and lower stem of wheat, reducing nutrient uptake and plant vigor.
Wheat___Common_Root_Rot.symptoms: Brown lesions on roots and crown area, yellowing of lower leaves, stunted plant growth, reduced tillering, and premature death of plants. Infected roots appear dark and decaying.
Wheat___Common_Root_Rot.treatment_prevention: Use certified disease-free seed, apply seed treatments (fungicides), practice crop rotation (at least 2 years), avoid waterlogged soils, maintain proper soil drainage, and use balanced fertilization.

Wheat___Fusarium_Head_Blight.description: Fusarium head blight (scab) is caused by Fusarium graminearum. It infects the wheat head during flowering, producing toxins that make grain unsafe for consumption.
Wheat___Fusarium_Head_Blight.symptoms: Bleached or premature whitening of spikelets, pink or orange spore masses on infected spikelets, shriveled and lightweight grain (tombstones), reduced test weight, and mycotoxin contamination (deoxynivalenol/DON).
Wheat___Fusarium_Head_Blight.treatment_prevention: Plant resistant varieties, apply fungicides at early flowering (anthesis), avoid planting after corn or other crop residues, tillage to bury crop debris, and ensure good field drainage.

Wheat___Healthy.description: The wheat plant appears healthy with no visible signs of disease or pest damage. The leaves are green, vibrant, and free from spots, lesions, or discoloration.
Wheat___Healthy.symptoms: No symptoms. Leaves are uniformly green, stems are strong and upright, and the plant shows normal growth and development.
Wheat___Healthy.treatment_prevention: Continue good agricultural practices: proper irrigation, balanced fertilization, crop rotation, and regular field monitoring to maintain plant health.

Wheat___Leaf_Blight.description: Helminthosporium leaf blight is caused by Bipolaris sorokiniana (formerly Helminthosporium sativum). It causes necrotic lesions on leaves that can merge and kill entire leaf blades.
Wheat___Leaf_Blight.symptoms: Elongated, oval to rectangular brown lesions with dark borders on leaves. Lesions may have a tan center. Severe infections cause leaves to wither and die from the tip downward.
Wheat___Leaf_Blight.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties, apply fungicides when disease is detected, practice crop rotation, use certified clean seed, and maintain balanced soil fertility.

Wheat___Leaf_Spot.description: Leaf spot on wheat is a general term for several fungal diseases including Helminthosporium leaf blight and Tan spot. They cause necrotic lesions on leaves that reduce photosynthetic area and yield.
Wheat___Leaf_Spot.symptoms: Tan to brown oval or elongated lesions with yellow halos on leaves. Lesions may merge, causing leaf yellowing and premature death. The disease thrives in no-till systems with crop residue.
Wheat___Leaf_Spot.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties, apply foliar fungicides, practice crop rotation, use certified clean seed, maintain balanced fertilization, and consider tillage to bury crop residue.

Wheat___Mite.description: Wheat mites (such as wheat curl mite and brown wheat mite) are tiny arachnids that feed on plant sap. They cause discoloration, leaf curling, and can transmit viral diseases.
Wheat___Mite.symptoms: Fine stippling (white or yellow dots) on leaves, leaf curling and distortion, bronze or silvery appearance of leaves, dried leaf tips, and reduced plant vigor. Severe infestations cause leaf death.
Wheat___Mite.treatment_prevention: Use miticides for severe infestations, control weeds that serve as mite hosts, plant early to avoid peak mite populations, use resistant varieties, and maintain adequate soil moisture.

Wheat___Pest.description: Wheat pests include aphids, mites, and other sap-sucking insects that feed on plant sap, causing discoloration, leaf curling, and reduced plant vigor. They can also transmit viral diseases.
Wheat___Pest.symptoms: Yellowing and curling of leaves, fine stippling or silvering on leaf surfaces, presence of small insects on the underside of leaves, stunted growth, distorted leaf tips, and honeydew residue.
Wheat___Pest.treatment_prevention: Encourage natural predators (ladybugs, lacewings), apply insecticidal soap or neem oil for minor infestations, use systemic insecticides for severe outbreaks, control weeds, and practice crop rotation.

Wheat___Mildew.description: Powdery mildew is caused by the fungus Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici. It produces white, powdery fungal growth on the surface of leaves, stems, and sometimes heads.
Wheat___Mildew.symptoms: White to grayish powdery patches on the upper surface of leaves. Affected areas may yellow and die. Severe infections reduce photosynthesis, causing yield loss and weakened grain filling.
Wheat___Mildew.treatment_prevention: Plant resistant varieties, apply fungicides (triazoles or strobilurins) early, ensure good air circulation, avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, and practice crop rotation.

Wheat___Septoria.description: Septoria leaf blotch is caused by Septoria tritici. It is a major foliar disease of wheat, producing irregular necrotic lesions with visible black fruiting bodies (pycnidia).
Wheat___Septoria.symptoms: Irregular, tan to brown lesions on leaves with dark specks (pycnidia) visible within the lesion. Lesions expand and merge, causing premature leaf death. Lower leaves are affected first.
Wheat___Septoria.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties, apply foliar fungicides at flag leaf emergence, practice crop rotation, avoid planting infested residue, and maintain balanced fertilization.

Wheat___Smut.description: Wheat smut is caused by fungal pathogens (Urocystis tritici for flag smut, Tilletia caries for bunt). They replace grain kernels or leaf tissue with black, powdery spore masses.
Wheat___Smut.symptoms: Black, powdery spore masses replacing normal plant tissue. Flag smut produces long, dark streaks on leaves and stems. Loose smut replaces grain heads with masses of black spores.
Wheat___Smut.treatment_prevention: Use certified disease-free seed, apply seed treatment fungicides, plant resistant varieties, practice crop rotation, and remove infected plants before spores spread.

Wheat___Stem_fly.description: Stem fly (Meromyza saltatrix) is a pest that lays eggs in wheat stems. The larvae feed inside the stem, causing structural damage, reduced nutrient transport, and dead hearts (dead central shoot).
Wheat___Stem_fly.symptoms: White or transparent streaks on leaves, dead hearts (withering of the central shoot), stems that break easily, reduced grain filling, and presence of small white larvae inside the stem.
Wheat___Stem_fly.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties, apply systemic insecticides, practice crop rotation, remove crop residues, and monitor fields during the larval stage.

Wheat___Tan_spot.description: Tan spot is caused by Pyrenophora tritici-repentis. It produces tan-colored lesions with yellow halos on leaves, reducing photosynthetic area and yield.
Wheat___Tan_spot.symptoms: Tan to brown oval lesions with yellow halos on leaves. Lesions may have a dark center. Severe infections cause leaf chlorosis and premature leaf death. The disease thrives in no-till systems with crop residue.
Wheat___Tan_spot.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties, apply fungicides, tillage to bury crop residue, practice crop rotation, and maintain balanced fertilization.

Wheat___Yellow_Rust.description: Yellow rust, also known as stripe rust, is caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici. It produces yellow to orange pustules arranged in linear stripes along leaf veins.
Wheat___Yellow_Rust.symptoms: Yellow to orange pustules arranged in long, linear stripes along leaf veins. Leaves may curl and die prematurely. Severe infections reduce photosynthesis and grain filling.
Wheat___Yellow_Rust.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties, apply fungicides (triazoles or strobilurins) early, avoid susceptible varieties, practice crop rotation, and monitor fields during cool, wet weather.

Wheat___Rust.description: Wheat rust is a group of fungal diseases caused by Puccinia species (including stem rust, leaf/brown rust, and stripe/yellow rust). They produce colored pustules on leaves and stems, disrupting nutrient transport and reducing yield.
Wheat___Rust.symptoms: Orange, brown, or reddish-brown pustules on leaves, stems, and leaf sheaths. Pustules rupture to release powdery spores. Severe infections cause premature leaf death, stem weakening, and reduced grain filling.
Wheat___Rust.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties, apply foliar fungicides (triazoles or strobilurins) at early infection stages, practice crop rotation, destroy volunteer wheat and alternate hosts, and monitor fields regularly during warm, humid conditions.

Maize___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum. It produces large, cigar-shaped lesions on leaves, especially in cool, wet conditions.
Maize___Northern_Leaf_Blight.symptoms: Large, elongated, cigar-shaped, grayish-green to tan lesions (1-6 inches long) on leaves. Lesions often start on lower leaves and progress upward. Severe infections can cause significant yield loss.
Maize___Northern_Leaf_Blight.treatment_prevention: Plant resistant hybrids. Apply fungicides (triazoles or strobilurins) when lesions appear. Practice crop rotation and reduce residue to minimize inoculum.

Rice_Add___Bacterial_leaf_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked stripes starting at leaf tips and margins, turning yellow-to-white wavy lesions along the leaf length. Droplets of bacterial ooze may appear on leaves in high humidity.
Rice_Add___Bacterial_leaf_blight.treatment_prevention: Use resistant rice varieties. Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization. Keep fields free of weeds and maintain proper water management. Drain fields if disease is detected early.

Rice_Add___Brown_spot.description: Brown spot is caused by the fungus Bipolaris oryzae. It thrives in nutrient-poor soils and high humidity, causing significant yield losses in rice.
Rice_Add___Brown_spot.symptoms: Small, oval to circular brown lesions on leaves with gray or white centers. Lesions may coalesce causing leaf yellowing and drying. Also affects glumes and grains.
Rice_Add___Brown_spot.treatment_prevention: Improve soil fertility with balanced fertilization (especially potassium and silicon). Use resistant varieties. Apply fungicides if severe. Ensure proper water management.

Rice_Add___Leaf_smut.description: Leaf smut is caused by the fungus Entyloma oryzae. It is a minor disease but can reduce photosynthetic area and grain yield in severe cases.
Rice_Add___Leaf_smut.symptoms: Small, dark brown to black raised spots (smut pustules) on the upper surface of leaves. Spots may be circular or angular and often appear in groups. Leaves may turn yellow around lesions.
Rice_Add___Leaf_smut.treatment_prevention: Use disease-free seeds. Maintain proper field sanitation by removing infected debris. Balanced fertilization and proper water management reduce disease severity. Fungicide application is rarely needed.

Tea___anthracnose.description: Tea anthracnose is a fungal disease (typically Colletotrichum species) that causes irregular necrotic patches on tea leaves. It spreads in warm, wet weather and can reduce leaf quality and yield.
Tea___anthracnose.symptoms: Irregular, brown to dark-brown lesions that may begin as small spots and expand, often following the leaf veins. Infected tissue can crack and drop out, leaving ragged holes. Young shoots and leaves are most affected.
Tea___anthracnose.treatment_prevention: Remove and destroy infected leaves and prunings. Improve air circulation through proper pruning and avoid overhead irrigation. Apply appropriate copper-based or systemic fungicides during wet periods, and avoid stress by maintaining balanced shade and nutrition.

Tea___algal_leaf.description: Algal leaf spot on tea is caused by the parasitic green alga Cephaleuros virescens. It is most common in humid, wet conditions with dense shade.
Tea___algal_leaf.symptoms: Rusty-red to orange-brown, raised, velvety or crusty spots on the upper leaf surface. Spots are roughly circular and may be surrounded by a yellowish halo. Severe infections cause premature leaf drop.
Tea___algal_leaf.treatment_prevention: Improve air movement and reduce shade/humidity through pruning. Avoid overhead irrigation. Apply copper-based fungicides, which are effective against algal spot, especially before or during wet seasons.

Tea___bird_eye_spot.description: Tea bird's eye spot is a fungal disease (Cercospora theae) that produces small, distinctive lesions. It is more common on mature, lower leaves in shaded, humid plantations.
Tea___bird_eye_spot.symptoms: Small, round spots with a dark center and a lighter margin, resembling a bird's eye. Spots may have a purplish-brown ring and a grayish center, and can merge into larger blotches on severe infections.
Tea___bird_eye_spot.treatment_prevention: Remove affected older leaves and improve sunlight penetration by pruning and reducing excessive shade. Avoid water stress and overwatering. Apply fungicides such as copper oxychloride if infections are widespread.

Tea___blight.description: Tea blight is a group of fungal diseases caused by Pestalotiopsis species, commonly described as brown blight or gray blight. They are among the most prevalent leaf diseases in tea plantations.
Tea___blight.symptoms: Irregular necrotic lesions that start as small brown or gray spots and expand into large blotches, often with concentric rings. Lesions may be dark brown (brown blight) or grayish with darker margins (gray blight). Severely infected leaves wither and drop.
Tea___blight.treatment_prevention: Prune and remove infected leaves and debris to reduce inoculum. Maintain balanced shade and nutrition to avoid stress. Apply appropriate fungicides (e.g., carbendazim or copper-based products) during wet, warm periods. Harvest promptly to reduce infection of young leaves.

Tea___healthy.description: The tea leaf appears healthy with no visible signs of fungal, algal, or bacterial disease.
Tea___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green color, intact leaf margins, normal vein structure, and no spots, lesions, or discoloration.
Tea___healthy.treatment_prevention: Maintain good plantation hygiene, balanced shade, and proper nutrition and irrigation. Inspect foliage regularly for early signs of pests or disease.

Tea___red_leaf_spot.description: Red leaf spot on tea is a fungal leaf disease that produces red-colored lesions. It tends to appear under warm, humid conditions and can reduce photosynthetic area.
Tea___red_leaf_spot.symptoms: Red to reddish-brown spots or blotches on leaves, sometimes with darker borders or a yellowish halo. Lesions may coalesce and cause leaf distortion or premature drop in severe cases.
Tea___red_leaf_spot.treatment_prevention: Remove infected leaves and improve air circulation through pruning. Avoid prolonged leaf wetness by limiting overhead irrigation. Apply appropriate copper-based or systemic fungicides during high-humidity periods.

Tea___white_spot.description: Tea white spot is a fungal leaf disease characterized by white to pale lesions. It is favored by cool, humid conditions and can affect leaf quality.
Tea___white_spot.symptoms: Small, white to pale-gray spots or lesions on leaves, often with a slightly darker or water-soaked border. Spots may enlarge and merge, causing chlorosis and leaf drop in severe infections.
Tea___white_spot.treatment_prevention: Remove and destroy infected foliage. Improve air flow and reduce humidity through pruning. Apply fungicides preventively in cool, wet weather and maintain balanced plantation nutrition.

Cacao___anthracnose.description: Cacao anthracnose is a fungal disease (Colletotrichum species) that attacks cacao leaves, causing necrotic lesions. It is favored by warm, wet weather and can weaken young trees and reduce pod set.
Cacao___anthracnose.symptoms: Irregular brown to dark-brown necrotic lesions that often start as small spots and expand along leaf veins. Infected tissue may crack and fall out, leaving ragged holes. Severe infections cause leaf yellowing and premature defoliation.
Cacao___anthracnose.treatment_prevention: Remove and destroy infected leaves and pruning debris. Improve air circulation by pruning overcrowded canopies and provide proper shade management. Apply copper-based or systemic fungicides during wet periods, and maintain balanced nutrition to reduce stress.

Cacao___healthy.description: The cacao leaf appears healthy with no visible signs of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease.
Cacao___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green color, intact leaf margins, normal vein structure, and no spots, lesions, or discoloration.
Cacao___healthy.treatment_prevention: Maintain good plantation hygiene, proper shade management, and balanced nutrition and irrigation. Inspect foliage regularly for early signs of pests or disease.

Chilli___anthracnose.description: Chilli anthracnose is a fungal disease (Colletotrichum species) that attacks chilli leaves and fruit, producing sunken necrotic lesions. It thrives in warm, humid, rainy weather and can spread rapidly through the crop.
Chilli___anthracnose.symptoms: Circular to irregular dark-brown or black sunken lesions on leaves and fruit, often ringed with a yellow halo. Infected fruit develops concentric rings of spores and may shrivel or drop prematurely. Heavy leaf spotting leads to yellowing and defoliation.
Chilli___anthracnose.treatment_prevention: Remove and destroy infected plant debris and practice crop rotation. Improve airflow by proper spacing and avoid overhead irrigation. Apply copper-based or systemic fungicides during wet spells and use resistant chilli varieties where available.

Chilli___healthy.description: The chilli leaf appears healthy with no visible signs of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease, or pest damage.
Chilli___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green color, intact leaf margins, normal vein structure, and no spots, lesions, curling, or discoloration.
Chilli___healthy.treatment_prevention: Maintain balanced nutrition and irrigation, keep the field free of weeds and plant debris, and inspect plants regularly for early signs of pests or disease.

Chilli___leaf_curl_virus.description: Chilli leaf curl is caused by begomoviruses transmitted by whiteflies. Infected plants show severe leaf distortion and stunting, and the disease is a major constraint on chilli production in tropical regions.
Chilli___leaf_curl_virus.symptoms: Upward and inward curling and crinkling of young leaves, thickened and reduced leaf blades, yellowing along veins, and stunted, bushy plant growth. Flowers and fruit are reduced, leading to significant yield loss.
Chilli___leaf_curl_virus.treatment_prevention: Control whitefly vectors with yellow sticky traps, reflective mulch, and appropriate insecticides. Remove and destroy infected plants early to reduce inoculum. Use resistant varieties and avoid planting near infected crops.

Chilli___leaf_spot.description: Chilli leaf spot (often Cercospora or Alternaria species) is a fungal disease that produces distinct spots on chilli leaves, especially in warm, humid conditions.
Chilli___leaf_spot.symptoms: Small circular to angular pale-brown or gray spots with darker margins scattered over the leaf surface. Severely affected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, weakening the plant and reducing yield.
Chilli___leaf_spot.treatment_prevention: Remove infected leaves and debris, rotate crops, and improve field ventilation. Avoid overhead irrigation and apply protective or systemic fungicides when conditions favor disease. Maintain balanced nutrition to keep plants vigorous.

Chilli___whitefly.description: Whiteflies are small sap-sucking insects that infest chilli leaves. Heavy feeding weakens plants, and whiteflies also transmit viruses such as chilli leaf curl, making them a serious pest of chilli crops.
Chilli___whitefly.symptoms: Small white-winged insects and pale nymphs clustered on the undersides of leaves. Leaves develop yellow mottling or silvering, become sticky with honeydew, and may grow sooty mold. Severe infestations cause leaf drop and stunted growth.
Chilli___whitefly.treatment_prevention: Monitor with yellow sticky traps and inspect leaf undersides regularly. Use reflective mulch to repel adults, apply insecticidal soap, neem oil, or targeted insecticides, and conserve natural enemies. Remove heavily infested plant parts promptly.

Chilli___yellowish.description: A yellowish appearance of chilli leaves is a general symptom that usually indicates nutrient deficiency, water stress, or a viral infection rather than a single pathogen. The pattern and distribution of yellowing help identify the cause.
Chilli___yellowish.symptoms: Leaves turn pale yellow or yellow-green, often starting between veins or on older leaves. Interveinal yellowing, yellow veins, or uniform yellowing may appear depending on the underlying cause, sometimes accompanied by reduced growth.
Chilli___yellowish.treatment_prevention: Diagnose the specific cause: test soil and apply balanced fertilizer for nutrient deficiencies, correct irrigation and drainage for water stress, and manage virus vectors such as whiteflies. Remove affected foliage and maintain overall plant health.

Turmeric___aphids_disease.description: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that colonize the undersides of turmeric leaves. Heavy feeding weakens the plant, distorts new growth, and the sticky honeydew they excrete encourages sooty mold, which can reduce photosynthesis.
Turmeric___aphids_disease.symptoms: Clusters of small green, yellow, or black insects on leaf undersides and young shoots. Leaves curl, yellow, or become distorted, and affected areas may feel sticky with honeydew and develop a black sooty mold coating.
Turmeric___aphids_disease.treatment_prevention: Inspect leaf undersides regularly and remove heavily infested leaves. Encourage natural predators such as lady beetles and lacewings, apply insecticidal soap or neem oil, and use water sprays to dislodge colonies. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization that promotes soft, aphid-friendly growth.

Turmeric___blotch.description: Turmeric blotch is a fungal leaf disease that produces irregular, diffuse discolored patches on the leaf surface. It spreads in warm, humid conditions with frequent leaf wetness and can cause premature yellowing and leaf dieback.
Turmeric___blotch.symptoms: Irregular, water-soaked to brown or gray blotchy patches on leaves, often merging into larger areas of dead tissue. Surrounding leaf tissue may yellow, and severely affected leaves dry out and die back from the tips or edges.
Turmeric___blotch.treatment_prevention: Remove and destroy infected leaves and debris, improve spacing and airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation. Rotate crops and apply protective or systemic fungicides when humid, wet weather favors disease. Maintain balanced soil nutrition for vigorous growth.

Turmeric___healthy.description: The turmeric leaf appears healthy with no visible signs of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease, or pest damage.
Turmeric___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green color, intact leaf margins and tips, normal vein structure, and no spots, blotches, yellowing, curling, or insect damage.
Turmeric___healthy.treatment_prevention: Maintain balanced nutrition and irrigation, keep the field free of weeds and plant debris, ensure good drainage, and inspect plants regularly for early signs of pests or disease.

Turmeric___leaf_spot.description: Turmeric leaf spot (often caused by fungal pathogens such as Cercospora or Colletotrichum species) produces distinct spots on turmeric leaves, especially under warm, humid, rainy conditions.
Turmeric___leaf_spot.symptoms: Small circular to oval brown, gray, or pale spots with darker margins scattered across the leaf surface. Spots may enlarge and merge, causing surrounding tissue to yellow and leaves to dry out or drop prematurely.
Turmeric___leaf_spot.treatment_prevention: Remove and destroy infected leaves and crop debris, rotate crops, and improve ventilation by proper spacing. Avoid overhead irrigation and apply protective or systemic fungicides when conditions favor disease. Maintain balanced nutrition to keep plants healthy.

BlackPepper___healthy.description: The black pepper leaf appears healthy with no visible signs of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease, or pest damage.
BlackPepper___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green color, intact leaf margins and tips, normal vein structure, and no spots, yellowing, wilting, mottling, or insect damage.
BlackPepper___healthy.treatment_prevention: Maintain balanced nutrition and consistent moisture, keep the field free of weeds and plant debris, ensure good drainage, and inspect plants regularly for early signs of pests or disease.

BlackPepper___leaf_blight.description: Black pepper leaf blight is a fungal disease that produces spreading brown or black lesions on leaves, often under warm, humid, rainy conditions. Severe infections can defoliate the vine and reduce yield.
BlackPepper___leaf_blight.symptoms: Irregular water-soaked to dark brown or black lesions along leaf edges or across the surface, often with yellow halos. Lesions enlarge and merge, causing leaves to curl, wilt, and drop prematurely.
BlackPepper___leaf_blight.treatment_prevention: Remove and destroy infected leaves and crop debris, improve air circulation with proper trellising and spacing, and avoid overhead irrigation. Apply protective or systemic fungicides when wet weather favors disease and ensure good drainage.

BlackPepper___yellow_mottle_virus.description: Black pepper yellow mottle virus (Piper yellow mottle virus) is a viral disease transmitted by insect vectors and infected planting material. It causes a distinctive yellow mottling of leaves and can seriously weaken the vine over time.
BlackPepper___yellow_mottle_virus.symptoms: Irregular bright yellow mottling or mosaic patterns on leaves, sometimes with leaf distortion, curling, or reduced leaf size. Severely affected vines show stunted growth and reduced yield.
BlackPepper___yellow_mottle_virus.treatment_prevention: Use virus-free certified planting material and control insect vectors. Remove and destroy infected vines to reduce spread, and avoid pruning or tools that can transmit the virus between plants.

ginger___healthy.description: The ginger leaf appears healthy with no visible signs of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease, or pest damage.
ginger___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green color, intact leaf margins and tips, normal vein structure, and no spots, yellowing, wilting, or insect damage.
ginger___healthy.treatment_prevention: Maintain balanced nutrition and consistent moisture, keep the field free of weeds and plant debris, ensure good drainage, and inspect plants regularly for early signs of pests or disease.

ginger___leaf_blight.description: Ginger leaf blight is a fungal disease that produces spreading brown or dark lesions on leaves, often under warm, humid, rainy conditions. Severe infections can defoliate plants and reduce rhizome yield.
ginger___leaf_blight.symptoms: Irregular water-soaked to dark brown or black lesions on leaves, often with yellow halos, that enlarge and merge. Severely affected leaves turn yellow, dry out, and may drop prematurely.
ginger___leaf_blight.treatment_prevention: Remove and destroy infected leaves and crop debris, improve spacing and air circulation, and avoid overhead irrigation. Apply protective or systemic fungicides when wet weather favors disease, rotate crops, and ensure good drainage.

ginger___dehydrated.description: Dehydrated ginger plants show moisture stress. Leaves wilt, droop, and become dry and crispy at the margins and tips, usually during prolonged dry periods, heat, or poor irrigation.
ginger___dehydrated.symptoms: Drooping and wilting leaves with dry, brown, crispy margins and tips; leaf curling and reduced growth. Prolonged stress causes yellowing and premature leaf death.
ginger___dehydrated.treatment_prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture with regular, even irrigation and mulching to reduce evaporation. Provide shade or windbreaks in hot conditions, improve soil water retention with organic matter, and monitor soil moisture regularly.

ginger___pest_damage.description: Ginger leaves damaged by insect pests such as leaf-feeding caterpillars, thrips, and beetles. Feeding damage reduces photosynthesis and can weaken plants and open wounds for disease.
ginger___pest_damage.symptoms: Irregular holes, notches, chewed edges, and skeletonized areas on leaves, sometimes with visible insects, eggs, frass, or small necrotic feeding spots and silvery streaks from thrips.
ginger___pest_damage.treatment_prevention: Inspect plants regularly and remove visible pests and infested leaves. Use appropriate, registered insecticides or bio-pesticides targeted at the specific pest, encourage natural predators, and keep the field free of weeds and debris that harbor pests.

bean___healthy.description: The bean leaf appears healthy with no visible signs of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease, or pest damage.
bean___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green color, intact leaf margins and tendrils, normal leaflet structure, and no spots, yellowing, powdery growth, or insect damage.
bean___healthy.treatment_prevention: Maintain balanced nutrition and consistent moisture, keep the field free of weeds and plant debris, ensure good drainage and air circulation, and inspect plants regularly for early signs of pests or disease.

bean___downy_mildew.description: Downy mildew of bean is a fungal disease favored by cool, humid conditions. It causes pale yellow-green patches on the upper leaf surface and a gray to purplish fuzzy growth on the underside, reducing photosynthesis and yield.
bean___downy_mildew.symptoms: Pale yellow or light green angular blotches on the upper leaf surface with a grayish-purple downy growth on the underside; leaves may curl, yellow, and drop prematurely in severe infections.
bean___downy_mildew.treatment_prevention: Use resistant or tolerant varieties, ensure good air circulation and spacing, avoid overhead irrigation in cool weather, rotate crops, and remove infected debris. Apply registered protective fungicides when conditions favor disease.

bean___leafminer.description: Leafminer larvae of flies tunnel between the upper and lower leaf surfaces, creating visible serpentine mines. Heavy infestation reduces leaf area for photosynthesis and can weaken plants.
bean___leafminer.symptoms: Winding, whitish or pale serpentine tunnels (mines) across the leaf blade, sometimes with small dark feeding punctures and stippling; severe damage causes leaf browning and premature drop.
bean___leafminer.treatment_prevention: Inspect plants regularly and remove and destroy mined leaves. Use yellow sticky traps to monitor adults, encourage natural enemies and parasitoids, and apply registered insecticides or bio-pesticides targeted at leafminer larvae when infestations are high.

bean___powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew of bean is a fungal disease that appears as a white, powdery coating on leaves, stems, and pods. It thrives in warm, dry days with cool nights and can reduce yield and pod quality.
bean___powdery_mildew.symptoms: White to light gray powdery fungal growth on the upper surface of leaves, stems, and pods; affected leaves may yellow, curl, dry out, and drop early in severe cases.
bean___powdery_mildew.treatment_prevention: Use resistant varieties, provide good air circulation and spacing, avoid overcrowding, and maintain balanced nutrition. Apply registered sulfur- or fungicide-based sprays at first sign of infection and remove affected plant debris at season end.

cauliflower___healthy.description: The cauliflower plant appears healthy with no visible signs of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease, or pest damage.
cauliflower___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green leaves and curd, intact leaf margins and veins, normal head development, and no spots, yellowing, water-soaked lesions, or rot.
cauliflower___healthy.treatment_prevention: Maintain balanced nutrition and consistent moisture, ensure good drainage and air circulation, keep the field free of weeds and plant debris, rotate crops, and inspect plants regularly for early signs of disease.

cauliflower___black_rot.description: Black rot of cauliflower is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris. It enters through leaf margins and water pores, producing V-shaped yellow lesions that darken as veins turn black, and it can destroy the crop under warm, humid conditions.
cauliflower___black_rot.symptoms: Yellow V-shaped lesions at leaf margins that progress toward the leaf center, blackened leaf veins, wilting and yellowing of leaves, and in severe cases head infection and plant death.
cauliflower___black_rot.treatment_prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and treat seed with hot water, practice crop rotation of 2-3 years, avoid overhead irrigation, control cruciferous weeds, remove infected debris, and apply registered copper-based bactericides at the first signs.

cauliflower___downy_mildew.description: Downy mildew of cauliflower is caused by the oomycete Peronospora parasitica. It thrives in cool, moist conditions and produces pale patches on the leaf upper surface with a gray-white fuzzy growth on the underside.
cauliflower___downy_mildew.symptoms: Pale yellow-green irregular blotches on the upper leaf surface with a grayish downy growth on the underside; leaves may yellow, curl, and drop prematurely, and heads may become discolored in severe infections.
cauliflower___downy_mildew.treatment_prevention: Use tolerant varieties, ensure proper plant spacing and air circulation, avoid overhead irrigation in cool weather, remove infected leaves and debris, rotate crops, and apply registered protective fungicides when conditions favor disease.

papaya___healthy.description: The papaya leaf appears healthy with no visible signs of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease, or pest damage.
papaya___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green color, intact leaf margins and veins, normal palmately-lobed leaf structure, and no spots, yellowing, curling, mottling, or powdery growth.
papaya___healthy.treatment_prevention: Maintain balanced nutrition and consistent moisture, ensure good drainage and air circulation, keep the field free of weeds and plant debris, and inspect plants regularly for early signs of disease.

papaya___anthracnose.description: Anthracnose of papaya is a fungal disease caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. It thrives in warm, humid conditions and produces dark, sunken lesions on leaves, petioles, and fruit, reducing photosynthesis and fruit quality.
papaya___anthracnose.symptoms: Circular to irregular brown to black sunken spots with concentric rings on leaves and petioles; pinkish spore masses may appear in wet weather, and fruit develops water-soaked, sunken lesions that rot.
papaya___anthracnose.treatment_prevention: Use disease-free planting material, provide good air circulation and spacing, avoid overhead irrigation, remove and destroy infected leaves and debris, apply registered protective and systemic fungicides at early stages, and practice field sanitation.

papaya___bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of papaya is caused by bacterial pathogens that enter through wounds and natural openings. It produces water-soaked lesions that yellow and later turn brown, reducing leaf area and weakening the plant.
papaya___bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that enlarge and turn yellow to dark brown or black; spots may coalesce, causing blighting and premature leaf drop.
papaya___bacterial_spot.treatment_prevention: Use disease-free seeds and planting material, avoid overhead irrigation and work when leaves are wet, remove infected plant parts, practice crop rotation and field sanitation, and apply registered copper-based bactericides at the first signs.

papaya___curl.description: Papaya leaf curl is a viral disease (papaya leaf curl virus) transmitted by whiteflies. It causes severe leaf curling and crinkling, stunted growth, and reduced fruit production.
papaya___curl.symptoms: Downward curling and crinkling of leaves, thickened and deformed veins, vein clearing, stunted plant growth, reduced leaf size, and in severe cases leaf yellowing and premature drop.
papaya___curl.treatment_prevention: Control whitefly vectors with appropriate insecticides or bio-pesticides and reflective mulches, use healthy seedlings, remove and destroy infected plants and alternate weed hosts, install yellow sticky traps for monitoring, and avoid planting near infested fields.

papaya___ring_spot.description: Papaya ringspot virus (PRSV) is transmitted by aphids and is one of the most destructive diseases of papaya. It causes mottling, ring spots, leaf distortion, and severe fruit and yield losses.
papaya___ring_spot.symptoms: Yellow mottling and mosaic patterns on leaves, thin chlorotic ringspots on fruit, leaf distortion and reduced leaf size, stunted growth, and in young plants severe wilting and death.
papaya___ring_spot.treatment_prevention: Use resistant or tolerant varieties, control aphid vectors with registered insecticides and reflective mulches, rogue and destroy infected plants, remove alternate weed hosts, and replant in clean fields away from infected orchards.

okra___healthy.description: The okra leaf appears healthy with no visible signs of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease, or pest damage.
okra___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green color, intact leaf margins and veins, normal palmately-lobed leaf structure, and no spots, yellowing, curling, mottling, or powdery growth.
okra___healthy.treatment_prevention: Maintain balanced nutrition and consistent moisture, ensure good drainage and air circulation, keep the field free of weeds and plant debris, and inspect plants regularly for early signs of disease.

okra___alternaria_leaf_spot.description: Alternaria leaf spot of okra is a fungal disease caused by Alternaria species. It thrives in warm, humid conditions and produces small circular to irregular brown-to-dark lesions on leaves, reducing photosynthesis and weakening plants.
okra___alternaria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Small water-soaked lesions that enlarge into brown to dark necrotic spots with concentric rings and yellow halos; heavily infected leaves yellow and drop prematurely.
okra___alternaria_leaf_spot.treatment_prevention: Use disease-free seed, practice crop rotation, improve air circulation, avoid overhead irrigation, remove infected debris, and apply registered fungicides at the first sign of disease.

okra___cercospora_leaf_spot.description: Cercospora leaf spot of okra is a fungal disease caused by Cercospora species. It causes small angular brown-to-gray spots with darker borders, mainly on older leaves, and can defoliate plants under wet conditions.
okra___cercospora_leaf_spot.symptoms: Angular to irregular brown or gray spots with reddish-brown margins on leaves; spots coalesce, leaves turn yellow and drop, reducing yield.
okra___cercospora_leaf_spot.treatment_prevention: Space plants for good airflow, avoid wetting foliage when irrigating, rotate with non-host crops, remove and destroy infected plant residues, and apply protective fungicides when conditions favor disease.

okra___downy_mildew.description: Downy mildew of okra is caused by the oomycete Pseudoperonospora species. It develops under cool, humid conditions and produces pale-green to yellow angular lesions with a downy, grayish spore growth on the lower leaf surface.
okra___downy_mildew.symptoms: Pale yellow angular blotches bounded by veins on the upper leaf surface, gray-white downy growth underneath, and premature leaf yellowing and shedding in severe cases.
okra___downy_mildew.treatment_prevention: Improve ventilation, avoid prolonged leaf wetness by irrigating early in the day, remove infected leaves, rotate crops, and apply appropriate fungicides preventively during humid periods.

okra___leaf_curl_virus.description: Okra leaf curl is a viral disease transmitted by whiteflies. It causes severe leaf curling, vein thickening, stunting, and reduced fruit production, and can spread rapidly through a field once whitefly populations are established.
okra___leaf_curl_virus.symptoms: Upward or downward curling and crinkling of leaves, thickened and darkened veins, yellowing, stunted plant growth, and malformed or reduced fruit.
okra___leaf_curl_virus.treatment_prevention: Use resistant or tolerant varieties, control whitefly populations with sticky traps and approved insecticides, remove and destroy infected plants early, and avoid planting near heavily infested fields.

okra___phyllosticta_leaf_spot.description: Phyllosticta leaf spot of okra is a fungal disease caused by Phyllosticta species. It produces pale-brown to tan circular spots, sometimes with dark borders and tiny fruiting bodies, and can cause premature leaf drop under moist conditions.
okra___phyllosticta_leaf_spot.symptoms: Circular to oval pale-brown or tan spots with darker margins and small black fruiting bodies; spots may dry and fall out leaving shot-hole damage, leading to defoliation.
okra___phyllosticta_leaf_spot.treatment_prevention: Remove infected leaves and debris, improve airflow between plants, avoid overhead watering, rotate crops, and apply fungicides at early symptom development when needed.
